0: A customer-service call ends. Was the user's problem solved? Did the agent miss an important condition? When there are few recordings you can listen to them one by one; once there are many, manual spot-listening struggles to cover every call.
1: Traditional quality review relies mainly on manual spot-listening, which takes a lot of time and hardly covers all calls. Using speech recognition and audio multimodal models, you can analyse the call content, speakers, emotion, service tone and how the two sides interact, and then have a large language model score the call against the review rules and produce a review report.
2: This chapter takes one customer-service call from a language training institution and runs the whole path from recording to review report.
4: Different business scenarios have different expectations of service quality. Before automating the review, be clear about which questions the review should cover and set the corresponding rules according to the actual business requirements.
6: A language training institution's customer service usually handles course enquiries, class-start notices, leave requests, course changes, learning feedback and after-sales matters over the phone.
7: In the review you need to check whether the agent understood the customer's needs correctly, whether the answers were complete and accurate, whether unresolved questions were given a follow-up, and whether there were improper promises. The service attitude and the interaction also affect quality: for example, whether the agent was impatient, perfunctory or blaming, whether the customer was interrupted, and whether the customer showed negative emotion.
8: That information cannot come from the transcript alone; it needs the speakers plus the emotion, tone and interaction in the recording.
10: Once the scenario requirements are clear, organise them into concrete review rules: which items a call must be checked against, and the scoring standard for each, as the basis for automatic judgement and scoring later.
11: Following the service requirements of a language training institution's phone support, the rules cover need response, information accuracy, problem resolution, service attitude, call behaviour and customer emotion, as in the table below.
16: Whether the agent greets first, states the institution and their own identity, and asks what the customer needs
18: Need recognition and completeness of response
19: Whether the customer's questions are identified and each is answered effectively
22: Whether uncertain information is invented, and whether there are improper promises about learning outcomes
24: Problem resolution and closure of promises
25: Whether the customer's core problem is resolved, and whether a follow-up is explained when it cannot be resolved immediately
27: Whether there is impatience, blame, perfunctoriness, abuse or shifting of responsibility
29: Whether the customer is interrupted frequently, talked over, or the rhythm clearly harms communication
32: Whether the customer shows clear negative emotion and whether the agent explains and reassures in time
34: Whether the call is closed politely and outstanding items are confirmed
37: The automatic review later judges and scores each rule in turn. Different items need different information: need recognition, information accuracy and problem resolution are judged mainly from the call content, while service attitude, customer emotion and interruption need the recording analysed as well, and the results are then combined into the overall review.
39: Following the scenario requirements above, the system first obtains the call transcript and speaker information from the recording, then analyses customer emotion, agent tone and the interaction from the audio, and finally hands those results together with the review rules to a large language model for overall judgement, scoring and report generation. The whole automatic review process is shown below.
40: The process divides into two parts: call-data analysis and the overall review.
42: Once the recording enters the system, the audio format is normalised first, converting sample rate and channels into what the later models can handle.
43: The processed audio uses FSMN-VAD to detect the active speech regions and CAM++ to separate the speakers, giving each speaker's speaking time. What you get at this point are speaker ids such as spk0 and spk1, whose identities are not yet known.
44: Speech recognition uses Qwen3-ASR-0.6B. The model converts the recording to text and records the time span of each piece of text. Aligning the recognition output with the speaker analysis by time gives a transcript with speaker ids and timestamps. Then, from each speaker's dialogue, a smaller Qwen3-4B judges their role in this call and converts the speaker ids into “agent” and “customer”. 45: The audio also carries information that the text cannot show directly: the agent's emotion and service tone, changes in the customer's emotion and how the two interact. Qwen2.5-Omni-3B analyses the recording, together with the transcript, to judge whether the agent was impatient, perfunctory, blaming or curt, whether the customer showed clear negative emotion and whether the agent responded appropriately, and whether there was obvious talking over or interruption.

63: The normalised result keeps the complete transcript, the speaker roles and the combined speech analysis. Business content such as customer needs, completeness of answers, resolution, promises and compliance is no longer analysed separately in advance; the large language model judges it all together in the overall review from the complete call content.
65: After the call-data analysis, the review rules from section 20.1.2 and the normalised results go into Qwen3-8B together. The model judges from the complete transcript which needs the customer raised, how the agent responded and whether the problem was handled, and combines the agent's emotion and tone, the customer's emotion and the agent's response, and the call interaction to judge and score each rule.
66: For information that only the company's business rules can verify, such as course times and leave policy, if no corresponding business standard is supplied, the review only judges whether the agent gave a clear response, not whether the content is correct, and notes in the report that “the available information cannot be verified”.
67: The review scores each rule from section 20.1.2 in turn. Besides a score, each item must state the judgement and the main evidence. When a problem is found, cite the relevant turn of the call, the agent's words or the combined speech analysis as evidence, avoiding bare conclusions such as “poor attitude” or “problem not handled properly”.

70: Below we write the program following the technical plan above and implement the automatic customer-service review step by step.
73: Download the models in advance so later loading can use the local cache directly.
74: After installation, import the dependencies the program needs.
78: Convert the input recording to a uniform 16 kHz mono WAV.
79: Use FunASR with FSMN-VAD and CAM++ to get each speaker's speech segments and their times.
80: Use Qwen3-ASR-0.6B to recognise the whole recording, and ForcedAligner to get the timestamps of the recognised text.
81: Use Qwen3-4B to judge each speaker's role from their dialogue and convert the speaker ids into “agent” and “customer”.
82: The transcript with roles and timestamps is now available. Next, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B uses the recording to analyse further the agent's emotion and service tone, the customer's emotion and the agent's response, and the interaction between them.
83: For a long recording, feeding the whole audio into the model at once uses a lot of VRAM. Split the audio according to the call turns found earlier: rather than cutting at fixed times, wait until the agent's current turn has finished once a segment reaches the target length, so each segment keeps whole conversational content. Qwen2.5-Omni-3B is loaded once, analyses the segments in turn, and the results are organised by their time ranges.
86: Organise each module's results into a unified text format.
88: The normalised results and the review rules from section 20.1.2 go into Qwen3-8B, and the model analyses the call content and the analysis results together to score the call and generate the report.
90: The main program also needs a few helper functions to align the ASR text with speaker segments by time, build the complete transcript and save the review report.
